title: Self-management_(computer_science)
summary:
Self-management in computer science is the process by which computer systems manage their own operation without human intervention. Initiated by IBM in 2001, this initiative aimed to develop computer systems capable of self-management to overcome the rapidly growing complexity of computing systems management. This concept, often synonymous with autonomic computing, draws inspiration from the human bodys autonomic nervous system.

IBM defined four key functional areas for self-managing systems, often referred to as self-star properties. Self-Configuration is the automatic configuration of system architecture at runtime, enabling systems to adapt by adding, replacing, or removing components. Self-Healing is the capability to detect, diagnose, and repair malfunctions automatically. Self-Optimization is continuous improvement of nonfunctional properties such as performance or resource usage. Self-Protection ensures security by detecting and recovering from malicious attacks.

In a self-managing autonomic system, the human operator defines general policies and rules that guide the self-management process instead of controlling the system directly. The autonomic manager implements the Monitor, Analyze, Plan, Execute, Knowledge (MAPE-K) control loop, which is the core mechanism enabling autonomic behavior.

The increasing heterogeneity of corporate computer systems, the inclusion of mobile computing devices, and the combination of different networking technologies make conventional manual management very difficult, time-consuming, and error-prone. Real-world examples include Googles Borg cluster management system and Kubernetes, an open-source platform inspired by Borg designed for automating deployment, scaling, and operations of application containers.
